newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FEATURE-Kuwait "joke" candidate is best show in town.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Kuwait "joke" candidate is best show in town.

text.p: Odds are he might again win a few dozen votes but his jocularity and straight talk amasses the largest crowd of any of Kuwait's political rallies.

Mohammad Hafiti's popularity in Kuwait is spreading to neighbouring Gulf Arab states where video tapes of his hilarious election speeches fetch more than $60. Kuwait's parliament is the only elected house in a Gulf Arab state.
"If I become a minister I'll be at your service. But, if I become finance minister that would be a private issue," Hafiti told a large crowd of chuckling Kuwaitis at an election rally.
He is one of 240 candidates contesting for 50 parliament seats in the October 7 race, but few voters take him seriously although they flock to his night rallies for entertainment.
In the 1992 election Hafiti won some 50 votes.
With some 8,000 people in attendance, including women and youths -- both do not have the voting right -- restaurants use Hafiti's gatherings to hand out promotion leaflets.
Crowds gather early at his rallies to get a front row view, others stand on top of their cars to see Hafiti's in action.
"We are here to laugh. I heard a lot about him at school," said Ahmad Abbas, who is under the voting age of 21, as he and classmates sat waiting for Hafiti to appear.

Hafiti rose to the stage waving his hand like a world leader to the crowds which received him with loud applause, shrills and even kisses from male fans. Police cars flocked to the area to help unblock a traffic jam.
He could hardly finish a sentence from a prepared speech without being interupted by the giggling audience, asking one man "Do you want me to bite you?".
No public figure in Kuwait escapes his criticism, accusing deputies of sleeping in parliament after a free lunch, being paid hefty salaries and using their office to travel abroad.

"He (an MP) sits (in parliament) for four years eating while we stare into each others eyes," Hafiti said. "We have to hold MPs accountable...We want devoted MPs. We don't want them to sleep in the chamber. We don't want rubber stampers."
Hafiti says he is a firm advocate of women's right to vote and has a special tent for females at his rallies.
"Women lift weights and some of them wrestle also."
He wants the National Assembly to change its official name to "the assembly of deputies" because women, over 50 percent of the 700,000 Kuwaitis, cannot take part in the election process.
"If you want a real democracy give women their right (to vote)," said Hafiti touching on an issue that attracts the attention of many Kuwaitis and Western allies.
Unlike many candidates, Hafiti does not offer dinner to the crowd which sits on a rug-covered sand lot off a highway known as Democracy Road.
"It is good that you brought your dinner with you since you know that I do not offer dinners," Hafiti told a man whose mouth was full of food. "I'll give a dinner only after (I win)."
Mohammad al-Ajmi, 28, said at a Hafiti rally "His words have some truth in them but he exaggerates with satire. He is practising democracy in a cynical way."
Asked if he would vote for Hafiti, Ajmi echoed an answer given by many -- an outright "No".

A veiled woman who gave her name only as Umm Hussein said: "If I could vote I would vote for him. At least he is straight forward not like the deputies who promised to give women the right to vote and forgot their promises in the cosy chair."
But, some analysts say, Hafiti is tackling issues that serve the government's alleged goal of seeking a more docile house and suggest that he receives government support.
The government firmly denies any intervention in elections.
"In one word people come here because he is a joker," said a member of Kuwait's ruling al-Sabah family who sat in his jeep listening to Hafiti's speech blaring out of loudspeakers.
